doc.title: Joe LaBarbera interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 15, 2021

title: Explaining jazz to listeners and communicating with an audience
summary: He welcomes sincere lay listeners and teaches adherence to song form as the way to communicate.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Let’s pretend you’re at a cocktail party and you get in a conversation with a person you don’t know and they don’t know who you are, so if they ask you what you do, what’s the first thing you say?
I say I’m a jazz drummer.

And then they say, “Oh yes, jazz, well I like it until they start doing that stuff and then I don’t — what the heck are they doing? How do they know when to stop and start.” I mean do you try to answer or do you just go get another drink?

It depends. I mean if the person strikes me as someone that is actually being sincere I’ll spend some time and talk to them. In fact I really like hearing comments from people after gigs, they’ll come up and they’ll start out by saying, “I don’t know anything about jazz” or “this is the first time I’ve ever heard jazz.” But they’ll give me their impressions. And I would say nine times out of ten, their impressions are pretty accurate. All we need from a listener, from an audience, is a willingness to participate. A willingness to sit there and actually do what we’re doing, which is to tune in exclusively to the music. And just react to it. What are you feeling? I feel the same way when I go to a museum or an art gallery. I don’t know much about art but I can certainly have a reaction to what I’m seeing and I can certainly get a feeling from the music. It really is all about feeling. You can get a feeling from a painting, you can get a feeling from music. If you’re willing to go there and will let that happen then that’s all I ask of you.

I totally agree. I used to work with elementary school teachers, not music teachers. And they would make comments about music that I never would have thought of, they were so perceptive, and not with the music language. You know we usually speak in the music language and they had these other words and I said oh I have to take note of that. It’s very informing.

Yeah. Because at the end of the day it’s really all about communications. You might think you’re hip, you know, you might think you’ve got the greatest stuff on the planet to offer, but if you’re not communicating with an audience then I think it’s pointless. You need to get your music across to people.
How do you teach that to students?

It really starts basically with adherence to the song form. So if you’re connecting everything you do, whether it’s accompaniment or improvisation to a song form, right away you’ve made a connection to everything that’s going on. Now hopefully the band as a collective unit can get that point across to the listener. That’s — that’s as succinctly as I can put it because you know beyond that it’s really just doing it over and over again until you start to feel like you are getting a reaction from an audience for the appropriate

reason, you know, not because you played some blazingly fast single stroke rollover, or you were going crazy all over the drumset. The fact that you did something that communicated with the audience. And this gets back to those comments that I would get from lay people. People would say you know I could really hear you trying to help that soloist. That means more to me than anything else someone could say.
